query: Consider the following context: Melting properties are critical for designing novel materials, especially for discovering high-performance, high-melting refractory materials. Experimental measurements of these properties are extremely challenging due to their high melting temperatures. Complementary theoretical predictions are, therefore, indispensable. One of the most accurate approaches for this purpose is the ab initio free-energy approach based on density functional theory (DFT). However, it generally involves expensive thermodynamic integration using ab initio molecular dynamic simulations. The high computational cost makes high-throughput calculations infeasible. In that context, which method can be used for calculate its melting properties, including the melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at the melting point, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Applying a two‐phase coexistence simulation approach (such as using the interface pinning technique or the Z method) at the DFT level will yield reliable predictions of the melting temperature, entropy of fusion, enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at the melting point for refractory materials, while drastically reducing the computational cost compared to full thermodynamic integration via ab initio molecular dynamics.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high‐melting material modeled at the DFT level, prepared in a state that includes both solid and liquid phases near the melting condition.
generation.intervention: Simulate the material using a two‐phase coexistence method (e.g., interface pinning technique or the Z method) under DFT-level conditions.
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions at which the solid and liquid phases coexist in equilibrium near the melting point.
generation.structural_mediator: The interface where the solid and liquid phases coexist mediates the melting transition.
generation.mechanism: Direct equilibrium simulation of coexisting phases allows extraction of thermodynamic differences across the interface, thus determining the melting properties without the extensive integration over thermodynamic paths required in traditional methods.
generation.predicted_outcome: Accurate estimation of melting temperature, as well as entropy and enthalpy of fusion and volume change at melting, with a significant reduction in computational cost enabling high-throughput capabilities.
generation.baseline: The conventional ab initio free-energy approach using expensive thermodynamic integration via ab initio molecular dynamics.
generation.boundary: This method may be limited in systems that exhibit complex phase transitions or where the coexistence interface does not adequately capture all melting phenomena.
generation.uncertainty: While promising, the degree to which the two-phase coexistence approach maintains DFT-level accuracy across diverse refractory materials needs further validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct two parallel sets of DFT-based simulations on a refractory material: one set using the traditional full thermodynamic integration via ab initio molecular dynamics and the other using the two-phase coexistence simulation approach (via interface pinning or the Z method).
measurements: Volume change at the melting point
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the melting properties predicted by the two-phase coexistence approach differ by more than an acceptable tolerance (e.g., >10%) from those obtained via full thermodynamic integration, or if the computational cost does not show a significant decrease, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

A second prominent class of HEA systems are refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), which comprise mostly refractory elements and invariably crystallize as body-centered cubic ( bcc ) solid solutions; these alloys have been considered as promising candidate materials for elevated-temperature applications due to their exceptional resistance to softening and extremely high melting points [9] – [11] . The requirements for designing novel metallic alloys that are capable of surpassing a whole set of specific properties of currently available commercial alloys are, at present, a subject of high demand in the industry. For instance, an improved combination of metallic alloys should possess strength and ductility while maintaining a relatively low cost. This is especially true when one is dealing with materials for high-temperature applications. Therefore, new engineering solutions are needed for novel materials that outperform the capabilities of the currently used Ni-based alloys. One of the prospective innovative materials that could be able to meet the requirements of such demanding applications, especially in the aviation and aerospace industries, may be refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs). These are also known by other names, such as complex concentrated alloys (CCAs). These materials have been extensively studied in recent years [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ] due to their very interesting combination of properties in some of the compositions.

frame.goal: To predict the melting temperature along with associated thermodynamic properties (entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and the volume change upon melting) accurately.

frame.understanding: A promising alternative is the two‐phase (coexistence) simulation approach – such as the interface pinning technique or the Z method – which directly simulates a system with coexisting solid and liquid phases. decision.trend: Historically, researchers have relied on full ab initio free‐energy calculations combined with thermodynamic integration using ab initio molecular dynamics to compute melting properties. Although this approach reliably yields melting temperatures and related thermodynamic quantities (entropy, enthalpy and volume changes), its extremely high computational cost has made it impractical for high‐throughput screening. More recently, alternative techniques that simulate phase coexistence directly – such as the interface pinning method or the Z method – have been explored in model systems. These methods capture the melting process by simulating a system containing both solid and liquid phases in equilibrium, thereby reducing the need for extensive integration over thermodynamic paths while still maintaining accuracy for high‐temperature conditions.
decision.unsolved: A robust method that maintains DFT-level accuracy while drastically reducing the computational cost associated with full thermodynamic integration remains an open problem. In particular, efficiently and reliably extracting melting temperatures along with entropy, enthalpy of fusion, and volume change for refractory materials in a high-throughput framework has not yet been fully achieved.
decision.lever: two-phase coexistence simulation approach (e.g., applying the interface pinning technique or the Z method)
decision.why: This approach directly models a system with coexisting solid and liquid phases, allowing for extraction of melting properties from equilibrium simulations. It builds logically on past work by sidestepping the full thermodynamic integration route, thereby reducing computational cost while retaining the necessary DFT-level accuracy for high-temperature refractory materials.
